subject.title: [Security] Missing CSRF protection on local control plane HTTP routes

question: Should every state-changing Gateway HTTP request carrying a browser `Origin` be rejected unless that origin is explicitly allowed, including token- and password-authenticated requests, or is the current authentication-mode-dependent policy intentional?
rationale: The cited ACP modules are not vulnerable HTTP owners, while the real Gateway authorization layer deliberately applies explicit origin rejection only to selected authentication modes; changing that boundary could improve defense in depth but may affect supported browser clients and therefore requires security-owner intent.

options.title: Verify and document current model
options.body: Run focused cross-origin tests for each state-changing handler and auth mode, then close the report if foreign sites cannot supply the required credentials or bypass the existing origin gates.

options.title: Enforce origin uniformly
options.body: Reject disallowed browser origins before credential authorization for all state-changing HTTP routes, with allowed-origin configuration and compatibility tests for supported clients.

recommendation.title: Verify and document current model
recommendation.body: Run focused cross-origin tests for each state-changing handler and auth mode, then close the report if foreign sites cannot supply the required credentials or bypass the existing origin gates.

likelyOwner.reason: They merged and materially revised the closest existing Gateway browser-origin hardening and its regression coverage.
